beliefs.title: Make security understandable
beliefs.body: I want teams to understand what a control does and how to use it. Explain the risk in plain language, make the safe way practical and check that it works in day-to-day delivery.

beliefs.title: Give people clear ownership
beliefs.body: A review is one point in time. Someone still has to run the system, handle incidents and keep the controls working. I care about clear owners and a culture where people can raise a problem early.

beliefs.title: Look across five layers
beliefs.body: I work through identity, data, the model, the application and infrastructure. Who can act? What can they access? How can the model fail? What checks does the application enforce? Where does it run? This is a way to organise the review, not a compliance standard.

beliefs.title: Check what agents can actually do
beliefs.body: Documents and tool responses can contain hostile instructions. I check what happens if the model follows one: what data it could reveal, which actions it could take and where the application requires approval. A prompt alone is not an access control.

beliefs.title: Build compliance into the design
beliefs.body: For AI, data use and accountability need attention from the start. I bring privacy, retention, residency and evidence into the design, with legal or compliance specialists where needed. A completed checklist does not prove the system is secure.

beliefs.title: Use frameworks to guide the work
beliefs.body: NIST AI RMF helps organise risk decisions, OWASP helps identify application risks and MITRE ATLAS helps map threats. I use them to ask better questions, choose controls and record evidence, with findings an engineer can reproduce and fix.

writing.title: AI Security vs. Traditional Cybersecurity
writing.summary: Argues the two fields overlap rather than one containing the other, and explains why AI-specific risks still deserve separate attention. Short, opinionated, publishable as-is.

writing.title: How to Structure Security for a Big Organization
writing.summary: Lays out the functions every security org needs and the five structural models, then argues most orgs drift into a shape built by history rather than chosen on purpose. Well-sourced with external citations.
writing.src: How to Structure Security for a Big Org.txt

writing.title: What is a Forward Deployed Engineer
writing.summary: Explains the FDE role from its Palantir origins to the AI labs, and makes the security case that FDEs are an access-control problem as much as a delivery model. Well-sourced, no internal material.
writing.src: What is a Forward Deployed Engineer.txt

writing.title: Supply Chain and Dependency Compromises
writing.summary: Walks through every stage of an AI system, from training notebook to production jump host, mapping where supply chain compromise can enter. Detailed and technical.
writing.why_not: Reads as a chapter excerpt referencing figures and diagrams that are not included; needs rewriting as a standalone piece.

writing.title: AI Weaknesses in the Real World
writing.summary: Collects documented cases of AI systems being exploited outside research settings, from voice ID bypass to a chatbot selling a car for a dollar. Grounded in named public incidents.
writing.src: AI Weaknesses in the Real World.txt
writing.why_not: Claims about specific incidents (dates, companies, outcomes) are not independently verified here and should be fact-checked before publishing.

writing.title: Data Attacks
writing.summary: Explains how training data poisoning and feature manipulation compromise a model before it ever reaches production, mapped to MITRE ATLAS stages. Technically precise.
writing.why_not: Written as a chapter section referencing an unincluded system diagram; needs rewriting to stand alone.

voice_notes: She writes in short, direct sentences and states her own position plainly, often opening with 'I see' or 'I think' rather than hedging. She favours concrete, sometimes blunt framing ("the reason is blunt") over abstraction, and reaches for one clear metaphor per piece (a Venn diagram, a shape built by history) rather than stacking imagery. Technical pieces are structured and list-driven, mapping ideas to named frameworks like MITRE ATLAS. She rarely uses humour; the tone is measured and explanatory, closer to a briefing than a blog post. She cites sources plainly at the end of longer pieces rather than working links into the prose.

quotes.text: I see AI security and cybersecurity as overlapping fields, much like a Venn diagram.
The structure ends up reflecting yesterday's dynamics rather than today's operating reality: a shape built by history instead of chosen on purpose.
quotes.src: How to Structure Security for a Big Org.txt

quotes.text: The reason is blunt: the hard part of AI is not the model.
quotes.src: What is a Forward Deployed Engineer.txt

think_intro: Security should be straightforward enough for people to understand, own and run. This is how I approach the work.
topics_intro: Recurring themes in my talks, workshops and writing.
